subject: Post-demo: Integration decisions — chat vs completions & streaming semantics
messages:
From: Samir Patel <samir.patel@brightpath.ai>
To: rachel_kim@redwood.com
Cc: onboarding@brightpath.ai
Date: 2026-11-25T15:12:00-08:00
Subject: Thanks for the demo — a few integration questions

Rachel — thanks for the walkthrough today. The demo was helpful; a couple of follow-ups from our engineering and product teams so we can scope onboarding and the SOW: 

1) SDK and auth: which SDKs should we start with (Node, Python)? Do you recommend JWT-based service accounts or API keys for server-to-server calls when we deploy in our VPC? Any ephemeral token suggestions for client-side calls?

2) Routing & model selection: we plan to route high-priority customer-facing queries to a low-latency model and background reranks to a cheaper quantized variant. How do we express routing policies? Can we pin model versions per-route?

3) Structured output / tool calling: we want the assistant to call internal tools (ticket creation) and return JSON blobs with strict schemas. How deterministic is structured output with streaming enabled? Any tips for stop tokens and max_tokens to avoid truncated JSON?

4) Embeddings & rerankers: recommended embedding dimensionality and batching guidance — we expect 10k requests/day for embeddings and reranking for search. Also curious about tokenization differences between chat and completions endpoints and how they affect cost and max_tokens.

If you can reply with a short matrix or sample request/response examples (one chat with tool-calling example + one completion for single-shot generation) that'd be great. Also attaching the draft SOW so you can see scope.

Thanks — Samir
Samir Patel
Head of Product, BrightPath
From: rachel_kim@redwood.com
To: samir.patel@brightpath.ai
Cc: onboarding@brightpath.ai, michael_grant@redwood.com
Date: 2026-11-25T17:06:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Thanks for the demo — a few integration questions

Samir — great questions and thanks for sending the SOW. I pulled in Michael (platform) and Laura (solutions) to make sure we cover both infra and SDK-level guidance. High-level answers here; we'll follow up with a short doc and sample snippets.

Quick answers up front:
- SDKs: start with Python for backend ingestion and Node for any server-side JS services. Our SDKs are mostly thin wrappers — you can call the REST/HTTP directly if you prefer.
- Auth: For VPC/server-side, service-account JWT + short-lived tokens (we support exchange for ephemeral tokens) is recommended; API keys are supported for hosted use but less ideal for private deployments.
- Routing: yes — routes can be configured per API key or per route-id. You can pin model versions to an endpoint and configure fallbacks.
- Structured output & streaming: streaming will send partial tokens; we recommend emitting a final delimiter and validating against the schema on the client side. We have sample stop-token patterns and chunking advice below.
- Embeddings: batching 64–256 per call is usually efficient; we'll include cost/perf guidance.

Next steps: Michael will drop detailed examples (auth headers, cURL, request/response samples). Laura will propose a short call to review the SOW and confirm timelines. I've attached an integration checklist that maps SOW deliverables to tech tasks.

Best —
Rachel Kim
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: michael_grant@redwood.com
To: rachel_kim@redwood.com, samir.patel@brightpath.ai
Cc: laura_bennett@redwood.com, sergio_alvarez@redwood.com
Date: 2026-11-26T09:13:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Thanks for the demo — a few integration questions

Samir / team — digging into the specifics you asked for. I'm keeping this focused on reproducible patterns we use with customers.

1) SDK/auth patterns:
- Server-to-server (recommended): Create a service account in the Redwood Console -> issue a signed JWT. Exchange JWT for a short-lived bearer token (TTL 1h). Use the bearer token in Authorization: Bearer <token>. This allows us to rotate keys and integrate with your KMS.
- Hosted/non-sensitive client: API keys are OK but use a proxy to avoid leaking keys in client bundles.
- Example header: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1Ni...

2) Routing & model pinning:
- Routing rules are expressed as JSON policies in the console or via API: match conditions (route_id, metadata tags, geo) -> target model variant. You can pin by model_id + version_tag. If capacity is constrained, we auto-fallback to the next compatible quantized variant.
- Example: route "customer-chat" -> model "redwood-chat-13b:v2" with fallback "redwood-chat-13b-quant:v2".

3) Chat vs completions tokenization / semantics:
- Chat endpoint: uses conversation-aware token accounting (system+messages) and returns deltas when streaming. It's better for tool-calling and maintaining state; stop sequences can be token-aware markers (e.g., "###END###") rather than natural-language phrases.
- Completions endpoint: simpler single-prompt semantics and often slightly cheaper per-request for short single-shot tasks. Tokenization differences: both use the same tokenizer family but the chat API includes role metadata; effective max_tokens available to the model = model_max_tokens - prompt_tokens.
- Practical rule: prefer chat for interactive assistants and structured tool calls; prefer completions for single-shot templated generation.

4) Streaming & structured output considerations:
- Streaming returns partial text fragments. For strict JSON output, we recommend:
  a) Emit a preamble: "{"
  b) Stream complete string values and include explicit record delimiters: e.g., emit "<record_end>" after each object or a final sentinel like "###FINISH###".
  c) On the client, buffer until you detect the sentinel, then validate against your JSON schema.
- Use max_tokens conservatively; add a 10–20% headroom to avoid truncation mid-object. Example: if you expect 800 tokens of output, set max_tokens=1000.
- Stop sequences: use token sequences unlikely to be generated in normal text (e.g., "\n---END-OF-PAYLOAD---\n"). If you use user-facing stop words, streaming can stop early and leave broken JSON.

5) Embeddings & reranker guidance:
- We expose p50/p95 latency and tokenized sizes in the model profile. For batching throughput, we recommend batch sizes of 128 for CPU-based embedding workers and 256–512 for GPU-backed pipelines depending on vector dim.
- Use a lightweight prefilter (prefix/simhash) before reranking to reduce tokenization and cost. For reranking: run cheap vector similarity to pull top 200 then full-text rerank via a reranker model.

6) Sample snippet (curl) — chat with tool-calling (simplified):

curl https://api.redwood.com/v1/chat
 -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"
 -H "Content-Type: application/json"
 -d '{"route_id":"customer-chat","model":"redwood-chat-13b:v2","messages":[{"role":"system","content":"You are a ticketing assistant."},{"role":"user","content":"Create a ticket: subject=Payment failure, user_id=123"}],"stream":false,"max_tokens":800}'

Response (on success):
{
  "id":"resp_abc123",
  "object":"chat.completion",
  "choices":[{
    "message":{"role":"assistant","content":"{\"action\":\"create_ticket\",\"ticket_id\":\"T-71234\",\"status\":\"created\"}"},
    "finish_reason":"stop"
  }]
}

Notes: for streaming, that JSON would be emitted in chunks; include the sentinel at the end.

7) Stop / max_tokens interplay:
- If you set max_tokens too low, the model will truncate mid-value. If you rely solely on stop sequence without headroom, you risk incomplete output. Strategy: set max_tokens with headroom and enforce stop tokens to terminate early when correct.

I can produce a one-page matrix comparing chat vs completions costs and sample request/response bodies. Attaching sample-request-response-examples.txt with cURL and JSON examples.

-Michael
Platform Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Michael — that helps a lot. A couple of clarifications so our architects can sign off: 

- For the streaming + sentinel approach, does Redwood guarantee ordering of chunks and at-least-once delivery semantics for stream events? We need to make sure we don't lose the final sentinel in edge cases.
- For reranking: curious whether it's better to do sparse-retrieval + embeddings or dense-only. We currently do BM25 + FAISS; would you recommend replacing BM25 or combining?
- Can you share one example where stop tokens caused truncation in a customer deployment and how you mitigated it (post-mortem style)?

If you can share the one-pager and a short pairing session next week, we can finalize the SOW.

—Samir
From: laura_bennett@redwood.com
To: samir.patel@brightpath.ai, rachel_kim@redwood.com
Cc: michael_grant@redwood.com, sergio_alvarez@redwood.com
Date: 2026-11-27T09:03:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Thanks for the demo — integration decision & next steps

Samir — quick answers and proposed next steps: 

1) Streaming guarantees: we provide ordered, sequential shards for a single request stream and best-effort delivery; networks can drop the final frame in extreme cases. Mitigations we use with customers:
  - Emit a small final checkpoint payload (signed by server) that is idempotent so clients can request a replays endpoint for missing finalization.
  - Use a persistent log for critical ticket creation where the assistant returns a confirmation id that the client writes to your backend.

2) Retrieval + rerank recommendation: keep BM25 as a fast prefilter (cheap recall) and use FAISS/dense vectors for candidate expansion. Then run a reranker model on top of the merged candidate set. This hybrid approach reduces cost and improves recall.

3) Stop-token truncation example (brief): a customer used natural-language stop tokens ("Thanks!") and streaming with max_tokens set too low. The model emitted half the JSON and the client attempted to parse it, causing an incident. Fixes: increased max_tokens with 20% headroom, introduced sentinel tokens, and validated payloads server-side before actioning.

Action items:
- Michael to share the 1-page matrix and explicit cURL + streaming examples (attached).
- Rachel to schedule a 45-min technical review next week (please propose two times).
- Redwood to send a redlined SOW by 2026-11-30.

Would Tuesday 2026-12-01 10:00 PST or Wednesday 2026-12-02 14:00 PST work for you?

Thanks —
Laura Bennett
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
